title: Falls, access and mobility awareness
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose and limits of falls, access and mobility awareness
Apply the principle to a service-business situation

instruction.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instruction.heading: Instruction
instruction.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to maintain clear access and reduce falls risks while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Before moving equipment, identify mobility routes, ramps, walking aids, grab rails, loose mats, pets and changes in floor level. Ask the resident before repositioning furniture or personal aids. Keep routes clear and dry; do not leave cords, buckets or wet surfaces where a person may walk. Never assist with transfers or lifting a person unless specifically trained, authorised and equipped. If a fall occurs, follow the emergency response plan and avoid unsafe movement of the person.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A cleaner is asked to move a walking frame to reach a skirting board. They ask permission and arrange the work so the aid remains immediately available to the resident.

Guided practical exercise
Mark hazards on a sample home floor plan, set up a safe cleaning zone and demonstrate how to pause work when the resident needs to pass.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Protects mobility routes, seeks permission and responds to falls within authorised competence. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

procedure: Before moving equipment, identify mobility routes, ramps, walking aids, grab rails, loose mats, pets and changes in floor level.
Ask the resident before repositioning furniture or personal aids, and keep any aid immediately available to them.
Keep routes clear and dry, with no cords, buckets or wet surfaces left where a person may walk.
Confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation before acting.
If the task goes beyond your training, the consent given, safe access or the agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others, and report promptly.
Do not assist with a transfer or lift a person unless you are specifically trained, authorised and equipped.
If a fall occurs, follow the emergency response plan and avoid unsafe movement of the person.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems. Completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. Boom-type elevating work platforms need a high risk work licence in Victoria at any boom length, and in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania, the Northern Territory and Western Australia where the boom is 11 metres or more. The WorkSafe WA page (last updated 13 August 2026) and the NT WorkSafe bulletin (no date shown) both state the 11-metre threshold. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Queensland's definition does not cover platforms under 11 metres (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). Tasmania's WP licence applies where the boom length is 11 metres or more, and no licence is needed for a boom under 11 metres (WorkSafe Tasmania page, last updated 1 December 2023). In New South Wales and Queensland the boom length is 11 metres: a boom-type platform of 11 metres or more needs the licence, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. This lesson does not grant a licence. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory. Check the licence rules for your state or territory and obtain your employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

qualityStandard: Mobility routes, ramps, walking aids and changes in floor level are identified before equipment is moved.
Permission is sought before furniture or personal aids are repositioned.
Routes are kept clear and dry, with no cords, buckets or wet surfaces left in a walking path.
No transfer or lift is attempted without specific training, authorisation and equipment.
summary: Before equipment is moved, the cleaner identifies mobility routes, ramps, walking aids, grab rails, loose mats, pets and changes in floor level.
Routes are kept clear and dry, and cords, buckets and wet surfaces are kept out of walking paths.
Transfers and lifting are not done unless the cleaner is trained, authorised and equipped, and a fall is handled under the emergency response plan.

knowledgeChecks.question: What observable actions demonstrate that you can maintain clear access and reduce falls risks?
options: Leaving buckets and cords across the walking route so the client can see them
Lifting a resident to help them past the wet floor without any training or permission
Checking mobility routes and aids, keeping paths clear and dry, and asking before moving any aid
Moving a walking frame without asking because it is in the way and leaving it in the corridor

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you do when a walking aid blocks your route in a resident's home?
options: Keep the equipment in the route, since it is out of the way and the resident can walk round it
Move the resident's frame and return it later without telling anyone at all in the house
Continue until the resident asks you to stop and clean up the route afterwards
Pause the work, clear the route, and check with the resident or coordinator before continuing

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the lesson say to do before repositioning furniture or personal aids?
options: Move it and tell the resident later
